utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can everybody hear me? Prosecutor's office and the Defence as well? The Chamber issued an order dated today which I am going to read out. Pursuant to Rules 54, 65(bis), 71, and 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, (there is no copy of this) Noting the Status Conference held on 18th February 1998, and noting the request confidentially filed by the Prosecutor on 18th February 1998, and noting the Defence motion filed on 18th February 1998, and further noting the agreement given by General Blaskic given during the Status Conference, considering that Judge Riad, member of Trial Chamber I, presently in this case is not available due to illness, and considering that his unavailability should not prejudice the accused's right to be judged without undue delay, as provided by Article 21.4.C of the Tribunal’s Statute and considering the fact that Rule 74(a) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence gives leave to the Trial Chamber in exceptional circumstances and in the interests of justice, and upon 24 request by one of the parties, to order that a deposition be taken for use 25 at trial, and appoint for that purpose a presiding officer. Considering that the provision of Rule 71 is in all matters in keeping with the testimonies heard in court and provides for cross examination of the witness, and in keeping with Rule 71(e), the deposition and the record hereto related will be transmitted 6 to the full formation of the Chamber, noting that the Chamber believes that the unavailability of one of its members is an exceptional circumstance, and that it is in the interests of justice that the testimonies in the present trial be not suspended, noting the fact that the parties agreed on this procedure under Rule 71 of the Rules, by which Judges Claude Jorda and Mohamed Shahabuddeen shall be appointed as presiding officers and the procedure shall only apply to four specific witnesses, considering that the accused agreed to the said procedure. Further considering that the parties agreed on the protected 17 measures adopted by the Trial Chamber I pursuant with Rule 75. For the above grounds I grant the requests, filed by both parties and order that the hearings on Thursday, 19th February, and Friday, 20th February shall be held to hear the witnesses in the procedure provided by Rule 71. Claude Jorda and Muhamed Shahabuddeen, as presiding officers 25, are hereby mandated to organise the hearing in the following manner. The presiding officers and the parties will appear in civilian 2 clothes and the hearing will be public, subject to the measures provided for the witnesses being maintained. Lastly, the record will be transmitted to the Trial Chamber composed of its three judges pursuant to Rule 71(e) of the Rules. Done in French and English, the French version being 7 the authoritative version, signed: the Presiding Judge so we are now having the hearing on this basis, and I hope, Mr. Harmon, that you have explained all this to your witnesses so that they are not caught by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. This being so, if you all agree, failing any observations, we might take on the course of our work and it is understood that all this will be reported to Judge Riad, and should Judge Riad make any observation on the basis of our report, or upon reading the transcript, we would, of course, call the witness again in the coming days or weeks. So be it. Mr. Prosecutor, I think you have a protected witness, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, good morning Judge Shahabuddeen, good morning, counsel. The next witness and the witness who is to be deposed is a protected witness, and he will have visual distortion, face distortion, and a pseudonym. He will be referred to as, "Witness AA". To summarise, Mr. President, Witness AA is a Bosnian Muslim retiree who resided in the Kiseljak municipality in the village of Visnjica which was a mixed Croat and Muslim village, and if I could have the ELMO turned on, Mr. President, and Judge Shahabuddeen, for your orientation about where the events he will describe occurred, I have placed on the ELMO Exhibit 29D. That is on the screen now, and that will indicate both the village of Rotilj and the village of Visnjica. Now, this witness will describe the attack on the village of Visnjica which occurred on the morning of 18th April 1993. At the time of the attack this witness was a civilian. He was a Muslim as well. He will describe how the village was very lightly defended and swiftly overtaken by the HVO. He will testify that on the 19th and the 20th, the HVO soldiers entered the village and systematically set fire to most of the Muslim houses in the village. He will describe a killing of an unarmed civilian by HVO soldiers. He will describe how, after the attack, he and other Muslim civilians were removed from the village and taken to a location he refers to as, "the silos". He remained there overnight, as did a large number of other Muslim civilians who were there as well. While they were there the HVO came and took Muslim men from that location and took them and forced them to dig trenches. He will testify that the following day he returned to his village and he discovered the corpses of his nephew and his nephew's wife who had been killed by the HVO, of whom were civilians, both of whom were Muslims. He will then testify about burying his nephew and his nephew's wife and five other Muslim civilians and he will testify that he remained in the village of Visnjica until September of 1993 when two HVO soldiers ejected him from his house, set his house on fire and set his son's house on fire. He was then taken to the Kiseljak barracks where he remained for 14 days. He will describe the conditions in the Kiseljak barracks and he will testify that while there, on a daily basis, Muslim detainees were taken out by the HVO to dig trenches, and he was informed that one of those individuals was killed and three of them were wounded and he will identify those people. At the end of 14 days he was taken by the HVO to the village of Rotilj where he remained until September 6th 1994. He will describe the conditions in the village of Rotilj. He will testify that every day the HVO took people out of the village, Muslims and forced them to engage in trench digging and other types of forced labour, he himself included. Lastly, Mr. President and Judge Shahabuddeen, he will testify that while he was in Kiseljak engaged in a form of forced labour which was trash collection, he saw members of the HVO marching through town with a decapitated head of a Muslim on the end of a post, at the end of a pole, with other members of the HVO playing music and parading behind the man carrying the decapitated head on the post and this took place in the presence, in broad daylight in the middle of town in the middle of the HVO police and others. That is a summary, Mr. President, of his testimony. His testimony relates in the indictment to count 1, persecution, all paragraphs, paragraph 6.1 through 7; counts 2-4, unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects, which is paragraph 8, counts 5 through 7, wilful killing, which is paragraph 9 of the indictment; counts 11 through 13, the destruction and plunder of property, paragraph 10; count 14, destruction of institutions dedicated to religion, paragraph 11; I am sorry, counts 15 through 18, inhumane treatment of detainees and hostages, paragraphs 12 through 15. Now, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, I would ask that you receive Exhibit 75, a copy of which I have provided to Mr. Dubuisson. It is an aerial view that depicts virtually all the areas that will be testified about by this witness. It depicts the village of Visnjica, Rotilj and the Kiseljak barracks, and you have that at your side for the purposes of assisting you understanding his testimony. Lastly, Mr. President, because the witness is a protected witness, I have instructed him during this deposition not to identify by name his relatives who were murdered by the HVO. He is prepared to do so, Mr. President, in a private session, but in a public session I have instructed him to only refer to them as his nephew and his nephew's wife. He will also be referring to his daughter only as his daughter, but if the court wishes or if counsel wishes to have them identified by name he is prepared to do so, but in a private session. That concludes my opening remarks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. We are going to let Witness AA come in. Please, when you put your questions, do not repeat what the witness said, whatever the witness said he would have said. I want to us speed up the proceedings, so let us have the witness in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, sir? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you are going to be heard as a witness. We shall call you, "Witness AA". Please check that your name is written on the piece of paper handed in by the Registrar. Do not mention your name, just wave or make a sign to show that it is your name. Fine. You agree to coming to testify in front of this Chamber, sitting today in plain clothes for reasons set out to you by the Prosecutor, but this does not change anything to your testimony. First, you are going to swear the oath which is in the same way as every witness does. Just remain seated, and you can read out in your own language the document that is being handed in to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have my glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take your time. (Pause). Please, go ahead. Do read out the oath. WITNESS AA (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Some preliminary questions will be put to you by the Prosecutor but soon thereafter you will be free to relate the events that have been summed up by the Prosecutor in relation to the events you were unfortunate enough to witness. You were not a victim of these events, but you witnessed them in Kiseljak. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness AA. Now, Witness AA, please, during the course of the questions I ask you, I would like you to relax, be calm and if you need a break, please let me know or let the court know. Let me begin. I am going to begin by asking you a series of very short questions and then I am going to ask you to give your answers in a narrative form about a number of subjects, but let me begin by asking you some background questions. How old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Bosnian citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April of 1993 were you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you live in the Kiseljak municipality in the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Until April, or until 1993, had you lived in Visnjica all your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was your village, Visnjica, a mixed Muslim and Croat village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was. Yes, a mixed village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, your village was attacked by the HVO on 18th April 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, at 5 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, before we get to the events of the attack, could you tell the judges anything unusual that you observed before the attack took place on the 18th April? Any unusual activity that may have suggested an attack was coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see about three or four days earlier people in uniform, two to three soldiers, and they were carrying automatic rifles in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And please continue just telling the judges who they were, what kind of uniforms they were wearing, what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniforms. On their arms they had the HVO sign, only I cannot remember on which arm they had this sign. They were walking by, and then I saw them digging trenches just above the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the response of the Muslims in the village when they saw the HVO digging trenches above the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people were going for negotiations, to negotiate that they fill in these trenches, but they said that they would remain there for the future, but this was a mere formality, they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many days before the attack started were those trenches dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some five to six days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned seeing men in HVO uniforms walking through the village. Who were they and what was their position in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were going by, and I saw them, and I saw somebody called Nikica Pravdic, called Braco, then Jelenko Pravdic, Drmac, Madin. Those were the ones I saw walking in uniform and carrying automatic rifles in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were any of those men commanders of the local HVO force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Nikica Pravdic, known as Braco, he was the commander of the HVO for the village of Visnjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness AA, very briefly, can you describe to the judges, first of all, if there was a Territorial Defence in your village, whether it was a large unit or a small unit, and whether it was well armed or poorly armed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several soldiers, like a detachment of Jasokovci. How many soldiers there were I do not know. I was not a participant. I was not a member. I was nothing. They may have been 10, 15 or 20, but I do not know that. The commander was Zijo Karahmet, captain first-class in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how would you describe their weapons, and the amount of ammunition they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very poor. If somebody bought himself something with his own money, then he had something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness AA, I would like to turn to 18th April 1993, and I would like you to tell the judges in your own words, at your own pace, the story of the attack on your village. Please begin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th April 1993 I woke up. I usually cannot sleep well, so I keep getting up and that day I got up at 4.30. I had two cigarettes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: got up and he said, "what is it, daddy?". I said, "Well, can you not hear the shooting, my son?", and he immediately ran into the room --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, are we talking about his son or his nephew, which is merely for the sake of precision?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are talking about his son at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, Mr. President? Witness AA, when you refer to relatives of yours, if you could just refer to them by a designation as, "my son", or, "my daughter", that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... and my son got up. He had a rifle. I think they called it a Sandzara, I do not know, and he ran off to the position he had, I do not know where it was. I did not see him again until April 1994 when I reached Fojnica. I never heard or saw him in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then this happened; there was an attack on the village. On the 18th, the 19th, I was in my own house. All that day I went out in the afternoon for a breath of fresh air, and a shell fell just in front of the house on the asphalt and two bits of shrapnel hit me in the back. They were not large but for me they were something. Then my daughter carried me inside, took me inside, and she treated and bandaged the wound. Before night-time the whole village, the younger people, women and children who were there, headed off towards Zeneca, the Kresevo municipality. I stayed on alone in the house. Nobody came. And then, in the morning, I was sitting there smoking, and then I hear somebody running and when I looked it was (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: are you going?", but he jumped over the fence and he had not reached 10-12 metres from my house when I heard somebody saying, "shall I get rid of him?", and another one answered, "get rid of him, fuck his mother", and a bullet hit him on the right-hand side and he fell to the left. I just did not see what part of the body it was, but it was his right-hand side. The person who had hit him ran up to him, and he took something from his pockets and put it in his own pocket. What it was, I could not see. Then he dragged him, maybe 25-30 metres away from my house, and he sort of shoved him to the side and he covered him with his jacket and went off. I went inside into my room and somebody came knocking at the door. "Who is there?", and I said, "me". He said, "come out here", and swore my bloody mother, and he said, "I am wounded. I cannot jump up so quickly", and then he repeated, "get out", shouting at me. So I started getting up from the couch I was lying on and I saw a barrel at the door. When I saw the barrel of a rifle I got up, and then I saw his head appear, and on his head was a helmet. I looked at him, and this is what I said to him, "Dusko, take care, I am wounded", and again he swore at me and said, "do not call me Dusko, you do not know who I am", but I do know exactly who he was and where he comes from. He forced me out of the house and he said, "you are going down to the mosque", and the distance is about 50-60 metres from my house to the mosque. "A car will come and take you away". When I got out of the house I told him I had a nephew around the back of the house. He allowed me to go to fetch my nephew. I was going, but he had his gun pointed at me. I opened the door of my nephew's house and called him out. "Come with me. I am being forced to go to the mosque and let us go together and then they will take us by car to the silo", and this nephew of mine answered, "uncle, good luck to you. I cannot even get up", because he was ill. He had problems with his spine. Then this one, this Dusko who was chasing me out, said, "come on", but I said to -- my nephew asked me to leave him a cigarette, if I had one, and so I had three or four cigarettes on me. I cannot remember exactly, so I put them on the table. Then he said he did not have anything to light them with, so I left him some matches, and I went off with Dusko following me. Dusko Prajo. He still had this gun pointed at me. About 20 or 25 metres from my house he said to me, "you see those people over there next to the mosque, you go there because I am going back to collect some more. Do not look around, left or right", so slowly, with a stick, I walked on and he left me. I did turn around a little, and I saw him going into the yard of my nephew's house. I stopped to light a cigarette, and I heard a rifle shot, somehow as if it was in a closed area. It was not in the open air, and then I went on as far as the mosque. Then the car came, we were loaded onto it and taken off to the silo. When we reached the silo and when we were coming out the HVO were selecting the younger people, and said to them that they had to go and dig trenches. They did not tell me, and they did not select me because I was elderly, but all the younger ones were taken aside. I spent the night there. In the morning when it dawned I had pains, and I saw an HVO soldier on guard duty, so I went up to him and said to him, "please, can I ask you something?", and he said, "yes. Do. Be free to ask me", and I said, "I am wounded. Could I go and see a doctor to take out the shrapnel, because it is hurting me", and he said, "go ahead grandpa, only I have no transport for you", so I headed off. I was about 20 or 30 metres away from him when I heard somebody saying, "halt, halt". I pretended not to hear, and then I heard the cocking of an automatic rifle and of course I immediately stopped, and again he swore at me and he said, "where do you think you are going?", and when I turned around to face him, it was Jozo Prankovic, known as Brico, and the guard was running after me, and he said to him, "Brico, I let him go to see a doctor, because he is wounded, to give him some first aid treatment", but he said, "I never asked you anything. You go back", and he would not let me go. So I went back. I sat there where the other people were. I do not know exactly, I did not have a watch, how long it was, or when it was, maybe it was just before noon, I headed home. I did not ask anyone, I just left. I needed to lie down. I could not stand it any more. When I went along the main road the cars passing by seemed to be heading straight for me, so I saw that I could not go any further, so I entered the field, but I followed the direction of the road and I reached my house. When I reached my house, I went immediately to see my nephew, how he was feeling. When I opened the door his bed cover was half on the floor, half on top of him. I called his name out from the door, "come on, get up. Let us have a cigarette". No reply. When I got in, my nephew was dead. Both he and his wife. He was already stiff. I saw that his left eye had been gouged out and his left arm, in the form of a pear, it was, so I opened up his shirt, a bullet had entered his chest. I went out. I went to the neighbours (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: sharply, "do you want to go to the cemetery for the killed to be buried? Where are you going to bury your nephew? If it is up to me to decide I will go and tell them where to bury him", and he allowed me to do that. I went to the cemetery with my cane, and when I got there there were six people digging, waiting for me to show them where, and so I pointed, "over there, please bury my nephew and his wife over there". Two of them started digging. They had dug about knee-deep, and then Nikica Pravdic, called Braco, came and said, "that is enough", and I answered, "Braco, the animals will dig them up". Again, he cursed me and he said, "I do not want to talk about it any more. That is enough". So, they brought in them on wooden planks, as we called them. We rolled them up in a blanket and put them there, and that is how it ended. Then the Doctors Without Frontiers came. Somebody had told them about me. Who it was, I do not know. They came to the door, knocking, and three of them walked in. One of them could speak our language, the other two could not -- my language. The one who could speak, he asked me how I was. I told him. They immediately put on white coats. I had to lie down, and they took out both of these two bits of shrapnel from my back. Then they sewed me up with four stitches for one wound and two for another, and they dressed my wounds every day for five days and they came every morning, bringing me food which was enough for the whole day, as I had no one to cook for me, so I stayed there, and that was how I recovered and I was at home until the 27th August 1993 when somebody knocked at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I want to say, before we get to 27th August 1993, let me ask you some questions to amplify and clarify parts of your testimony. You said that the HVO first enters your village on the 19th and more HVO came in on the 20th. Is that correct? 20th April 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what did you see HVO soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do not ask questions that have already been answered, Mr. Harmon. I am warning you. I shall interrupt you if you do so. You cannot say, "you said this, is this right?", because the witness is under oath, so the court is informed of what he said. Ask for precision only on those elements that have not been mentioned by the witness, otherwise I shall interrupt you. You cannot say to a witness, "you said this, is this right?". This is incompatible with judicial rules, because he is under oath. Only ask those questions that are necessary to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. I will rephrase my question, Mr. President. Witness AA, when the HVO soldiers came into your village on the 19th and 20th, what did you see them do to the Muslim houses that had been vacated by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see this. At first, they would load up the things, the furniture onto the vehicles, then they would take some liquid and pour all over and then they would light a match and throw it in there and everything would just be lighted up and burn down. I personally saw five or six houses as they poured some kind of liquid. I could not tell. I did not see what it was, but then he would just throw in a match and the house would go on fire. But first, they would take the furniture, and they would take it somewhere. I do not know where they took that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you see the HVO soldiers intentionally light on fire any Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No Croatian house was burned in my village. There were only two barns, two Croatian barns, that were burned in my village, but no houses. I saw that Selem Vulic's house was -- Mehmut, Elman, Mijo Pulja, Enes Begovic, Dzevad Celic, Meho Begovic, and Bajro, so those were the houses that I saw burning and I saw how they were -- they poured some fuel on them and then later I saw how they were burning my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, shortly after you returned to your village, following the attack, did you have an opportunity to walk around your village and count the number of Muslim houses, summer kitchens and barns that had been burned down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not right away, but about 20 days later, I think there were three or four of us, and we took a pencil and paper and we started walking from the top of the village to the bottom, and we were counting everything, and putting marks, and we counted all the houses, the barns, and the summer kitchens and altogether there were 103 burned structures. I saw that Ahmet Topalovic, Hamid Merdzanic and Sacir... these were all elderly men, and we went around, surveyed everything and wrote everything down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the 103 structures that had been burned, those were 103 structures that belonged to Muslims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to turn your attention to the testimony relating to the killing of Bajro Palavlija. Was that man a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bajro. Yes. He was Muslim, wearing civilian clothes, had no weapons on him, and he was going to search for his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the HVO soldier who killed him, can you identify him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Prajo, son of Jozo, from Kiseljak. I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned your nephew and your wife. Were they both Muslims? I am sorry, your nephew and your nephew's wife.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan Prijo, son of Jozo. He chased me and then he returned to my nephew's house, and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness AA, was your nephew and your nephew's wife, were they both Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Both of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you last left your nephew, did he have any weapons on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He had none. He was disabled. He could not move. He had nothing. He was just lying there, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you have testified about being taken to some silos. Where were the silos located in relation to the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bottom of the village of Visnjica. This belongs to an area, Visnjica Polje. That is part of the bottom part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to your return to your nephew's house, and the discovery of your nephew and your nephew's wife. While you were there, did you also come across a child of your nephew? And please, tell the court about that discovery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes, I did. I found him. He climbed from underneath the sofa and he said, "uncle, Dzono killed both my father and my mother". He was five years old. He was a boy, and when we heard -- Duzo was from Mostar and then later he came and took him and took him away and I do not know where he had taken him and I do not know anything about him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, just so that the record is perfectly clear, the man who you saw kill Bajro Palavlija, was he different than the man, the HVO soldier who came to your house and told you to go down to the mosque? Was that a different individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all wearing the same uniforms. No one else came. Just the one that I said. Dusan Prijo. Son of Jozo. And I did not see any other soldiers coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me turn your attention to that part of your testimony where you were present when a number of people were buried. Your nephew, and your nephew's wife were buried. Who were the other people? Can you identify them by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My nephew and his wife --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please listen, sorry, Mr. Harmon, I do not agree. Excuse me, Witness, let us start on solid foundations. We heard the testimony of Witness AA. If there are any challenges, either you ask for additional precision supporting the indictment, or else the court deems itself sufficiently informed. If there are challenges by the Defence, the Defence can, in its cross-examination, ask the questions and you have your additional interrogation. So unless you have precision that you are seeking which you did, on the child of the nephew and his wife, this is a new element, but if it is to just ask again for what has been said already, Judge Shahabuddeen and myself have heard that already, so let us not come back on this, otherwise we are going to double or triple testimonies. And we are going to devote too much them to them. Excuse me, Witness AA. It is a question of methodology. I have to make sure that the trial is being held in all due respect of the procedure, so, you gave as summary of what you were expecting from the witness, I have noted that down, so all that you mentioned has been said already, so let us not ask this additional questions of the witness. All you can do is bring precision, specifications and you have got, of course, the right to put questions once you have heard the cross-examination. So, Witness AA, carry on from that time on following the funerals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, I was attempting to make precision -- excuse me, Witness AA. With all due respect, Mr. President, I was attempting to make precision on the persons who were not identified who were buried with his nephew and the nephew's wife. The answer I was attempting to elicit was that the five other people were Muslims and they were all civilians and they included women. That is what I was attempting to elicit, Mr. President. That was not testified by this witness, and since we are dealing with an indictment that talks about attacks on civilians, that testimony should be part of this record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. As long as you do not have the witness repeat again what he has been through, and double it, so please, Witness AA, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which question? Shall I say who was buried on that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. The question is as follows, and then we will move on to the next sequence of events; were the people who were buried, were they Muslims? I am talking about the people who were buried with your nephew and his wife. You can answer that question and then the Prosecutor will ask you to move on to the next events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My nephew and his wife, that is two, are Bajro Palavlija, that is three, Senad Begovic, that is four, Palavlija Ago, five. Ismet Begovic, six. Seventh person was from Visegrad. He had come here to visit someone from the family. I do not know his first or last names. I only know that he was in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those people all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All civilians. Nobody wore any military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lastly, you have mentioned the name Nikica Pravdic who was an HVO commander in the village of Visnjica. Did you see him driving in stolen Muslim cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, in a white Lada and he changed cars every day, but I mostly saw him in a white Lada driving around, every day. And his house was right above my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the usher, if I could have Exhibit 73 placed on the ELMO, it is photograph Z1 bar 601. Witness AA, you will see this photograph on the ELMO and I am going to ask you to identify what that is. Can you identify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the mosque in Visnjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what happened to the mosque in Visnjica? What you saw happen to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw when they broke down the door, and they took everything away from the mosque, all furnishings. They first banged at the door. They could not break them down because they were iron. Then they brought an automatic rifle, so they shot through the glass first, and then into the lock where the key went in. Then they broke in and they took everything from it. It was just like bare floor left there, and they loaded it up on the truck. Where they took it, that I do not know. I do not know in which direction they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness AA, when you say, "they", who is, "they"? Can you identify them either in general terms or specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know when Jakov was banging with his foot, Franjo Skoro, he would run into it and kick it and then he also shot a burst of fire. Franjo Skoro, I knew him. I personally know that it was him. And the other four, those I do not know. They were wearing the uniforms and the HVO insignia but where they came from, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could continue with the story that you were telling the judges. You said that something happened on the 27th August when some soldiers came and asked -- and knocked on your door. Would you please continue with your story for the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th August 1993 I was sitting alone, below my house. It could have been between 10 and 11, around that time. I went into the bedroom to take a nap, and I fell asleep immediately. Then I heard someone knocking on the door, harder and harder, and then I responded, and I said, "it is me, who is there?", and the voice said "Open up". I said, "I am not going to open up to anyone at this hour", and he said, "you do not need to open up. Just give us over your daughter. Wake her up and make her come out", and I said, "she is not home"; "where is she?"; "she went to a party. She never came back home and I do not know where she is"; "Open up, open up so we can see". And I see that he was going to break in, so I took a risk and I opened the door. As soon as he walked in, he turned on the flashlight. There was no light, and I immediately saw who it was. Nenad Pravdic, Mico's son. "Where is your daughter?". He immediately went into her bedroom. He sees that the bedding was intact. "Where is she?", "I do not know. She went to some party. I do not know where she is. I do not know where she is staying the night"; "tell me where she is"; "I cannot tell you Nenad, where she is, when I do not know. She left before dark". "Come out with us". I went out with them. When I was out, I saw on the asphalt road that leads through Visnjica, there was a yellow Fiat, no registration plates. The door was open, and a man was sitting in and smoking. And then he says, "Nenad, fuck it, they will catch us". Who they were going to catch, I do not know. He turned to me and he cursed my bloody mother. He kicked me and he said, "go back into the house". So I stayed. I did not dare go back into the house. They left. So I ran into a small wood above the house and that is where I spent the night until dawn. That is where I was -- she came back in the morning, again, on the 29th. Again, they came knocking. I do not know who it is. Again, I respond. "Give me your daughter"; "she is not home. Did not I tell you that I do not know where she is? She is not sleeping at home". I knew where she was that night. "Open up, open up", and again, I opened up. They entered, they went straight to her room, they saw she was not there. They did not mistreat me, they left right away. In the morning, I got up, and I went to get her, to the place where she was spending the night, and as soon as I opened the door she said, like this, she said, "what is wrong, father?". I said, "nothing". "Something is wrong"; "no. Nothing is wrong". So this other woman came up where she had spent the night. Her husband, Fadil Topalovic, had been detained, and she said, "tell us where -- what is wrong?". Then I told them what happened. Then she started pulling her hair and said, "daddy, let us go wherever we can", and I said, "why do not we go home". She said, "no". That is how she told me. "Lets go home", and she just kept saying, "no". Then this other woman with whom she was staying said, "I am going to go with you too". So we came back home. I said, "daughter, just pick some good clothes and a travelling bag and we will get going", and then she started selecting her things. I did not interfere with that. At one point there was some crying and at the door my older daughter is at the door. "Daddy, what happened?". I told her, "I do not know what it is. They came looking for your daughter here"; "who?"; "those who came to you came to me as well". And so I went with her, I went to Nikica Pravdic, called Braco, the commander. He was not up yet, but his wife was, and I said, "please call Braco for me". She called him. He came to the door, and tells me, "what is up?", and I said, "Braco, give me some papers so she can go to Visoko, to my in-laws", and he said, "Oh come on, what are you talking about?", and he immediately went back into the house. So I moved on with her towards the village to another commander, Luka Drmac. He was also a commander. I also asked him to do that, and he said, "no, this is children. They are joking", and I said, "they cannot be joking". When this was Nenad, Mico's son. He turned around into the house, so that was the second one, Luka Drmac. I went to Franjo Skoro. He was a senior commander and I found his sister outside. I asked her, has Franjo gotten up? She said, "yes, he is there drinking coffee", and I said, "could you please call him for me?", and she said, "I can". She went and then she was gone for a while and eventually she is coming and Franjo is following behind her. He opens up the door, and he stopped at the door. He said, "what is up?", and I said, "please give me papers so that my daughter can go to Visoko to my relatives", and he said, "is that what you came for?" I said, "yes". Then he closed the door and went back into the house. I moved off from the house maybe twenty, twenty-five metres begging her to go back home. I said, "daughter, let us go back home", and she said, "daddy, you just go and best luck to you", crying. We parted, and I think we were maybe 10 metres away from each other. She said, "Babo, wait". She came over to me. "Daddy, will you do me a favour?", "yes", I said. "Come with me to Kiseljak"; "daughter, what are you going to do in Kiseljak when it is full of the HVO?". She had black skirt and black everything on. (11.30) In order to please her I went to Kiseljak. We did not talk during that time, and then we came to Kiseljak. It was full of the HVO, full of the uniforms. When we got there I knew where the police station was, so I went straight there. There was a policeman, a soldier there, and I said, "hello". He said, "hello, old man"; "can I talk to the commander?". He said that he had to ask. He went inside, and then he comes back out, and he said, "please come in, both you and your daughter". So we entered. He is standing by. "What is up, old man?", and I started telling him what happened to me and why I came. He said to the soldier, "do we have any cars free?", "take this, old man, and his daughter to the barracks, to room number 9". At that point I said, "can I ask you something?". And he said, "go ahead, ask". "You do not need to give me a car, just tell me where we should go, and to whom we should report". He said, "no, no, you have to go there by car". So they put us in this car, and we were driven directly to the barracks where the army is. We got out, and they said, "there is a bench over there, sit there. Do not look around and do not walk around. I am going to report", so we sat there. She kept crying, asking me, "what are they going to do to us, daddy?". I said, "daughter, I do not know. I know just as much as you". The building was maybe 2 metres away from where we were sitting. There were bars, and we could see many heads looking through the bars. Then this soldier who brought us came back and said, "sit there. Do not look around, do not move. A soldier will come for you", and he went off. "I am going to do my work". So we stayed there, and about five or six minutes later a soldier came with an automatic rifle, and he said, "grandpa, you and your daughter get up", so we got up. We were carrying this bag, and we were carrying it between us. We entered a corridor. It seemed to me to be a very long one, and then he said, "first door to the left". We got in. There were three soldiers in uniform with HVO signs. At one table, two of them, and at another table, just one. And then he said to me, "you, grandpa, sit at this table, your daughter next to you, and the bag next to her". So I sat down and she sat down. Nobody was saying anything. Then one of them got up and said, "do you smoke, grandpa?", and I said, "when I have anything, I do". So he opened a packets of cigarettes and offered me one, and a match, and I lit up, and I finished that cigarette. He did not ask me anything. Then he again got up and offered me a second cigarette, and I said, "Well, thank you, sir. I have just put one out"; "never mind. Have another one". So I took it and I lit it. I had smoked it maybe halfway, I was not really measuring, and he said, "are you feeling better now, grandpa?", and I said, "I am fine". He said, "we will not go into that". Then he said, "what is it that brings you here?". The other two sitting at the other table were not saying anything. They were writing something down. I do not know what they were doing. Then he kept asking me things and told him how things had happened, how they came looking for her and all these things, and then one of them, sitting to the side, said, "can I, commander, ask the old man just one question?". He said, "go ahead, go ahead"; "do you remember when this man knocked at your door and when you opened the door what his hair was like? Do you remember?". I said, "as far as I was able to say when he switched on his lamp he did not have much hair. It was very thin, here in front", and then he said, "sir, I know that he is telling the truth because I know the man. It is Nenad Pravdic". Then he asked my daughter, "young lady, do you know any people in Visoko or Fojnica, friends or relatives in that direction?", and she told him, "I do, in Visoko I have two uncles", and those were her mother's brothers. "So they are your mother's brothers, are not they? And where do they live?"; "they live in Bukovina"; "that is about 2 kilometres from Visoko. Would you like to go to your uncles?". She went on crying and then she asked me, "but what are you going to do, daddy?", and I said, "do not worry about me". Then this man got up and stroked her hair and said, "young lady, do not cry, whatever Mario can do, he will do for you", and when he said that, I realised who he was, Bradara Mario. I know his mother and his father and his uncle. I know them all. "Would you like to go to your uncles?", and then again she asked me what I was going to do and I said, "do not worry about me. Do not think about me. Just decide what you are going to do", and she chose to go and he immediately gave her a pass. At that moment the door opened. In came a man in black civilian clothes with a tie around his neck, a cigarette in his mouth. He wanted to shut the door, and he saw me. He caught sight of me. I have a nickname, (redacted) (redacted) Then this Mario said to him, "Bojo, I did not call you", and he pointed his finger that he should go out and he went. So he gave her this pass. He shook hands with us and wished my daughter good luck. We went out. He was running after us, and he called me, "grandpa!", we stopped. He said, "be careful in case Bojo comes across and mistreats you. I will escort you as far as the gate". We went as far as the gate. He entered the place where the police were and they talked. I do not know what they were saying, but anyway, he said, "a soldier will take you directly to the barricades", and that is how it was. A soldier came with a car, we got in, he took us to the barricade, she showed the pass, and they let her go and I went back. So, I did not know anything about whether she was alive or dead until the 22nd April 1994. I knew nothing about her. I stayed at home, the first, second and third and fourth. On the 4th in the evening, again someone came to my door, knocking. As he knocked, he also broke through the main door. I got up, I jumped up. Again, he switched on his lamp. I realised who it was, and he says, "where is your daughter?", and I said, "she has gone to Visoko". Then he cursed at me. "Did you send her away?". I said, "no, Bradara gave her the papers". Then he started hitting me, both of them. I cannot tell you what they did to me. They beat me up. I started bleeding. They were really hitting me hard. Then they dragged me outside, and Nenad Pravdic said, "fire!". Then this other soldier went to the house. I had a summer kitchen, and with incendiary ammunition they fired at the summer kitchen and it burst into flames and this other one went up the steps into my... I said, "do not set fire to at least one of the houses", my son's house, and again he cursed at me and he poured some liquid, I do not know which liquid, he poured this and then he said, "light it", and it went up in flames. Then I risked it. I said they would either kill me or they will throw me into the flames, so I thought I would jump over the fence and run into the field, and I escaped. The house was burning, and I escaped into the woods. That is where I was when it dawned, when day came on the 5th, the 5th September, I went back to my house, and I saw what had happened. What could I do? So I walked around among the remains and under my foot I felt something. It was a lighter. I wiped it off, and I saw what was written on it. And I put it in my pocket. It may be 10 or 20 minutes or maybe half an hour's time, I do not know, Nikica Pravdic, known as Braco, and another three soldiers from Travnik came up, and Pravdic Nikica asked me, "what happened here?", and I said, "Well, you see what happened"; "and who set fire to it?", he asked. "How do you expect me to know when it was after midnight?" And I had in my shirt pocket half a cigarette, maybe more, maybe less, and I took it out to light it, and I took out the lighter and I lit it and Pravdic grabbed that lighter from my hand. He snatched it away from me and I said, "do not take away that lighter, what am I going to use to light my cigarettes?". Again he cursed at me and he said, "I have seen this lighter somewhere. Let me check and then I will give it back to you". Nothing else happened. I walked around the village that day. On Monday 6th at dawn I was at a neighbour's house, and I was on my way home when I saw Braco, Nikica, in a car, and I stopped him. He stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness AA, why do you not just wait a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I was having a discussion with my colleague. It might be time for a break, for the interpreters' sake. I only wanted to know whether you had many questions to put to the witness. How long is the story going to take? A few minutes, or are we going to have the break right now? What do you think, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. President, insofar as the new portion of his testimony, I have two questions to ask him for clarifications, but the remaining part of his testimony will probably take 35-40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So it will not be 35-40 minutes. If I can make it shorter I will. So we are going to have to break now for twenty minutes: (11.50 am) (Short adjournment) (12.15 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness AA, two questions of clarification. That is Mario Bradara. Do you know what his position was in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that he was deputy commander, that is the deputy of the commander Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when -- the man who came to your house and set your house on fire on the 6th -- I am sorry, on the 4th September, were they wearing HVO uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, turning to the 6th September, can you tell the judges what happened to you and to other men, elderly men, women and children in the village of Visnjica, where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. Can I continue now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 6th September 1993 in the morning, about 9 o'clock, two buses came to the village of Visnjica, and they rounded up all the Muslims, they forced them out of their houses, those who were left, the women and children, and we were all boarded onto the buses, and we were driven off to Kiseljak. When you come to the turning for Rotilj, the buses stopped. Two policemen came in, and they put aside all the men, whereas the women and children went on to the village of Rotilj where there was a camp. We were taken off to the so-called barracks, and we were there. The younger men were selected for trench digging. I was not forced to go, because I am an elderly man. I was not forced to do that. They went off daily to dig trenches, and from the 6th September 1993 until the 20th September 1993 I was in the barracks, and then a car came, and the door of the room I was in was opened. I did not count. There were about 20, 25 or 30 of us there. I do not know how many. I was called out, and taken to the car. I got in, the door closed, and I was taken to Rotilj. We got to where Atif Hodzic's mill was. The car stopped there, the door was opened, and he just said to me "look for accommodation for yourself". He went off, he went back, and I stayed behind, and from there I looked around for somewhere to stay. Wherever you go and ask people it was all full, and at Sejo Dzina's I found room in the basement. I asked Sejo, "could I stay with you?", and he said, "you can, you can". So I stayed in his basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness AA, before we turn your attention to the events in Rotilj, I would like to stay and ask you some questions briefly about the conditions in the Kiseljak barracks where you and the other Muslims were detained. Can you describe to the judges with some degree of precision the conditions that existed, how many people there were in the Kiseljak barracks, how much food was given to each of the detainees, what sleeping conditions and quarters were available, whether anybody was killed in the process of digging trenches, whether the ICRC came to visit you. Could you please describe to the judges in some more precision answers to those particular areas I have identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. Yes. While I was in the barracks from the 6th-20th September 1993, we were in rooms in some rooms there were 20, in another, 30 people. I do not know exactly. As for food itself, we would get one loaf of bread of 750 grams which had to be shared sometimes by 12, sometimes by 14 people for a day. Then we get chicken liver paste, a small one, for four people and that was all we were given. That is as far as food is concerned. So it was poor in quality, and terribly small in quantity. Then the Red Cross came once, and we were taken out of the rooms, into the corridors, and they asked us, "do you have to work? What kind of food are you given? What about sleeping conditions?". Some people had a blanket, others did not have any. You would put your shoes under your head, if you had any, and that was it. When the Red Cross came and when they asked us what the food was like, "are you forced to dig trenches?", one of the people had the courage to say that the food was poor. Whether he took that down or not, I do not know. I did not see it, but when the Red Cross left he was beaten up terribly badly for having said that the food was no good. He was badly beaten up. They were taken to dig trenches every day. The younger men. I did not. I was not taken there. I can tell you that straight away. I know who the people were who went to dig trenches, and I know that Hasan Karahmet was killed while digging trenches. Another person who was wounded was Salko Sejdzic, and Avdo Palalija. Those were the men who were wounded. These two, whereas Hasan Karahmet was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness AA. Now, if you could please tell the judges about your experiences in the village of Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in the village of Rotilj, from 20th September until 21st April 1994, while I was in Rotilj the CARITAS organisation twice gave us 5 kilos of flour each and a large tin of canned food and a soap each. That was what we received until I was there, that was the 21st or the 22nd April 1994. There was very little food. What we ate most was potatoes. Potatoes. In 1994 on the 20th April we heard over the radio, Radio Kiseljak, that elderly people could go visit their family. So I immediately reported at the barricades and there Simo Komsic was there at the checkpoint from the village of Borni, and he asked me, "where are you going?". I said, "I heard last night on the radio that elderly people could go visit their family", and he said, "yes, yes, you are right"; "can I go then, Simo?"; and he said, "go ahead, only you have to go to the police first". So I went to Kiseljak, to the police station. The man on duty asked me, "what can I do for you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness AA, before you relate the events of leaving Rotilj, I would like to stay and have you describe further to the judges the conditions in Rotilj and specifically I would like you to describe to the judges the accommodations that were available to the Muslims, whether you were allowed -- whether Muslims were allowed to leave the village, whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to go anywhere. You could just walk around the village from one house to another. You were allowed to walk around, but not outside the village. You could not go anywhere. As for accommodation, I told you, some people had a cover given by their hosts or something to lie down on, and that is how we lived. That was the situation as it was while I was in Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the accommodations overcrowded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were up to 34 people in a single room in one house. The house had one floor, so there was nowhere to cook or to lie down. They would make a fire outside and then somebody would make some kind of a soup or stew, a vegetable stew, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there electricity and heating in the houses or was there no such luxury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no heating. If you had some timber you would light a fire. If you did not you just endure the cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the village of Rotilj, did the HVO come to the village every day and force Muslims to dig trenches and engage in other forms of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day they would come. Every day. In the morning, from 6.30 until 6.30 in the evening, when they would be brought back. They were taken to dig trenches every day, whether it was raining, whether it was cold or not, regardless of the weather, they went every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was it the HVO that would not let the Muslims leave the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. You could not go anywhere. It was not possible to go anywhere. Nor did you dare go anywhere out of the village of Rotilj. Only if you had an exchange arranged could you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what the HVO did to the livestock in the village and what they did to the money that some of the Muslims possessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for -- the whole village of Rotilj, there was not a single head of cattle or any animals, chicken or horses or cows. Nothing. They took everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the Muslim occupants of the village of Rotilj safe from physical attack while they were being kept in the village of Rotilj, or were they assaulted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would come in the evening. In the evening the HVO would come, looking for money, women. There are people that they took money from. They did not take any from me because I did not have any, but they did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were you forced to engage in some form of labour by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was forced by three or five days, I do not recall exactly, in Kiseljak to dump trash into a vehicle. On the 3rd January 1994 when I was in Kresevo Visoko intersection, I could hear a group of soldiers who were coming from the barracks. When they approached there were eight soldiers in uniform. One of them had an accordion on and was playing it. Three others had guitars and played and the others were shooting and singing and one of them, whose nickname was Pijuk, had a head stuck on a pole and they carried it. When I saw that, I had a heart attack. I was taken to the doctor's. His name was Pero Lovric and after that I was not taken to do any kind of labour any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness AA, the soldiers that were parading around with the decapitated head on a pole, was this in the centre of Kiseljak in the daytime or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Daytime. Daytime. They went through all of Kiseljak. They carried it through all of the town. I do not know where they brought it from, but they brought it from Kresevo, from some place called Cimpeno Brijek. I had never heard of this place before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you know or did you hear them say that the head on the post belonged to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said a balija. A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did the soldiers that you saw parading around the town, were they trying to conceal or trying to hide that head from the public and from the police and from others in the town, or were they quite proud and did they display it quite openly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Proudly. They went through all of Kiseljak and they played music and they carried it and they shot out of their weapons. Nothing was hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did any of the authorities, either the military authorities or the police authorities, stop them, arrest them, confiscate the head from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that. I was taken to the doctor's so I did not see whether they were stopped or prevented from anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And then eventually, and you can answer this with a yes or no answer, eventually you left Rotilj with a pass that permitted you to go visit relatives and you never then returned back to Rotilj. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. That is correct. When I went to the police, when I asked whether I could go and visit my family, I was told, I was asked, "when were you born?", and I said, "in 1927", and they said, "you can go for a visit"; "and where would you go?" I said in the direction of Visoko. They said, "you cannot"; "how about Fojnica?". They said, "you cannot". I said, "where can I go?". He then tells me Kiseljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness AA, based on those kind of conversations then you left the Kiseljak municipality and never returned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is correct. I never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, Witness AA. Thank you very much for your testimony. Mr. President, I have concluded my examination of Witness AA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Prosecutor. I suppose you want this document to be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That has already been tendered into evidence, Mr. President, that is Exhibit 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. I am now turning to the Defence and Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Witness AA. I would like to ask you, regarding the village of Visnjica, how many Croatian and how many Muslim homes were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. It was all mixed. I never counted how many of each there were, but it was all mixed. There were more Muslim than Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said today that there were 10-15-20 soldiers in your village. However, earlier you gave a statement and you said that there were 30 people in that unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not recall, because I was not a member of the Territorial Defence, or any army, so I did not count them, and so I could not clarify it for you. I simply do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But do you remember saying that there were 30 soldiers when you talked to the investigators of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been 20 or 30, 25. I did not count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, before this conflict, did refugees from Bilalovac, from the village of Pozetva near Konjic come to live in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly how many from Pozetva, but I know that there was one man with his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And did any -- the Muslims come from eastern Bosnia, from Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one who was from Visegrad, he came to visit his family as a member of the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But were there other Muslims who were there as refugees in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some from Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And do you remember that in July of 1993 some expelled Croats came from Fojnica, about 5,000 Croats in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5,000? That I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But this is in July of 1993 from Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the number which arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers Croats had in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly in April 1993 when the fighting started, when was it that it started, and when did the HVO enter the village, just so that we can clarify this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fighting started on 19th April 1993. I first saw the HVO soldiers with weapons entering at dusk on the 19th, some of them, and then on the 20th they all came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And when did the fighting start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At 5 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that before dusk on the 19th that Muslim civilians pulled out and later the TO soldiers pulled out of the village. Can you tell me in which direction they went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went towards Crnjici in the Kresevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know, the silo in your village when you mentioned, in January of 1993, a Muslim called Fejzic erected a barricade there and controlled the entrance to the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about the silo but I do not know who erected the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But was there a barricade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a little bit above the silo, about 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It was manned by the TO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So who was manning it? Who was controlling it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned Begovic, the man from Visegrad and so on, which were buried in that cemetery. Do you know under what circumstances were they killed? Did you see that? Or did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see how they were killed. I only saw how Bajro Palavlija was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. You answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The others I did not see being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that this HVO commander was driving in a white Lada. How do you know it was stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know who it was stolen from. Ibrahim Begovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned Rotilj and you said that it was a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did this camp have some kind of a fence around it which prevented people from leaving? How do you conclude that it was a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I concluded because I could not leave the village, because there was the army, the military was all around, so I could not leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that the person, nickname Pijuk, was carrying this head on a pole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of Maturica, which was a unit there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but Maturica -- I do not know the last name. He was from Brnjak, so I cannot tell you the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you know that he belonged to the Maturica unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Tihomil Blaskic? Do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him. I do not know him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that he is on trial here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I do not know anything about him. I do not know him, he does not know me. I cannot say anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But are you aware that he is on trial here now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, this completes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you want to give some precision?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Witness AA, on your direct examination you testified that the fighting in your village started the morning of the 18th April 1993 and on cross-examination, in response to one of Mr. Nobilo's questions, you said that the fighting started on the morning of the 19th of April 1993. Can you just think for a minute, concentrate, and could you clarify that point for us? Which day did it start? The 18th or the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO attacked the village of Visnjica on the 18th of April, and on the 19th, some entered the village but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness AA. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, you do not have any questions, do you? I do not either. You have been very accurate, Witness AA, and very thorough in your testimony relating these very painful events, and the Tribunal wants to thank you for coming here. You now can go home. You can try and find some peace and serenity. Do not move, please, for a while. We are going to suspend the hearing and this afternoon we are going to resume at 4 o'clock. Indeed, we have ex parte proceedings, starting at quarter to three. Thereafter we shall resume with the testimonies, at 4 o'clock. Tomorrow afternoon, there will be no hearing. I am saying this for the interpreters' sake, so tomorrow, I would like to start, if possible, at 9 o'clock, so that we can try and finish by 12.30. I invite the Prosecutor to make sure that the four witnesses do not have to spend the weekend here in The Hague, if that can be done. Thank you very much. The hearing is suspended. (12.45 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 20 21 22 23 24 25 (5.30 pm) (In Open Session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you have the accused brought in? (The accused entered court) First of all, I wish to reassure our fellow interpreters I am not going to be a tyrant and I also know that the accused has been waiting all afternoon, so I thought we should at least start with the next testimony. We will work until 6 o'clock, and tomorrow we shall resume at 9.15 instead of 9 o'clock. So without further ado, Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours, and counsel. The next witness is a protected witness. Mr. President, he has requested visual distortion and a pseudonym. He will go by the pseudonym of BB. Witness BB is a Bosnian Muslim who resided in Busovaca in the municipality of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Why do you not have AB? I thought it would be AB in the sequence. So are you going to have BB, CC and as follows? I mean it is not very relevant, but it is your choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I follow the wishes of the Registrar. I was told it was BB and I am happy to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. So Mr. MD will do as you wish, so as to Witness BB, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness BB is a Bosnian Muslim who is from Busovac municipality, from the village of Jelinak. He will testify, Mr. President, about four items. The first item he will testify about is that in January of 1993, the HVO disarmed the residents of the village of Jelinak and assured them that they would be protected if they surrendered those weapons. Secondly, he will testify about events which occurred on the 15th April 1993, when he and other Muslims from the village of Jelinak were arrested and taken to the Kaonik camp. Thirdly, he will testify that he was held in detention in the Kaonik camp from 15th April until 19th June 1993, and he will describe the conditions under which he was kept by the HVO, and he will identify a large number of locations, where he and other Bosnian male civilians were forced to dig trenches. Lastly, he will testify about seeing Dario Kordic in the camp at some point in time during his captivity. Those are the areas, a summary of what he will testify about. The counts in the indictment, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, are count 1 of the indictment, persecution, paragraph 6.4, 6.5, inhumane treatment of civilians, paragraph 6.7, forcible transfer of civilians. Then counts 15 and 16, the inhumane or cruel treatment of detainees, paragraphs 13 and 14. Counts 17 and 18, hostages which is paragraph 15, counts 19 and 20, human shields which is paragraph 16. That concludes my opening remarks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have written all that down, so I will be watching you. You mentioned four items. So let us have the witness in. Witness BB. So is he voice protected or is it only the face?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just the face, Mr. President, not the voice. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. We can start. Can you hear me now? The presiding judge is speaking to you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are going to be called Witness BB, but before that, you are going to identify your name but not speak it out. Identify your name on the document handed in by the Registrar. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you are going to swear the oath in your own language. You can read out the oath. Go ahead. WITNESS BB (sworn).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You agree to coming here on behalf of the Prosecutor in the trial against General Blaskic who is here present today. You have some preliminary questions asked by the Prosecutor in order to identify you, without you having to identify the hidden elements, and the Tribunal agreed to the protective measures concerning you. You are going to mention four items, the fact that the HVO disarmed the inhabitants of Jelinak, then you are going to speak to the Kaonik camp and the conditions in which you were kept after you were arrested, and also in which conditions you saw Dario Kordic, although I recall that this is not the trial against Kordic but against General Blaskic. So you have fifteen minutes for your preliminary questions, but the witness will come tomorrow again, but we will start with the testimony today now. You go ahead, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Witness BB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you some preliminary questions. First of all, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Bosnian citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1993, April, of that month, did you live in Busovaca municipality in the village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in fact you lived on the outskirts of that village, did you not?
