utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April of 1993 were you a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you, I am going to ask you about four sets of questions. The first is dealing with the January 1993 ultimatum and surrender of weapons by Muslims from the village of Jelinak, and in your own words, could you please tell the judges the circumstances under which the Muslims of Jelinak surrendered their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In January when the -- before the conflict I was supposed to go to my company to pick up my salary cheque, but however, I heard strong powerful explosions, and the shooting and I was -- I did not dare go there. The shooting was coming closer and closer to where I was, so that I started feeling fear. There were some people came, Muslims, and they said that we should have a meeting in the village of Jelinak. I went over there and the meeting was about the surrender of weapons. I did not know what it was, but they just said, "surrender of weapons". Then I saw that a certain Mario came. I do not recall his last name. He said to surrender weapons, and that they would guarantee safety. Again, the meeting resumed. We did not know what to do. Most of the people agreed to surrender weapons, and myself and a certain Jasmin did not want to surrender them. He had an automatic rifle which was issued to him in Zenica. It belonged to the Territorial Defence, that is the... And with me it was a bit different. During the fighting around Maglij with the Serbs I found this in a Serbian house and it was something that we called a "kubura". Then I saw Mario arriving with another two soldiers in a car, I do not know what make it was. There was a small quantity of weapons that displayed on the roadside. I started home. I was stopped at a point called Meraja. I was stopped by the HVO soldiers. They told me that supposedly I had to have some kind of a certificate to -- or let us say a pass from one point to another. I knew that I never needed one before, and then Stipo Andrijasevic came. He was also a local villager from the Jelinak. He was a local commander. Then he said, "there is no problem here, you can let him pass". I am sorry. Then he told me that we did well, and then I saw the village of Kovacevac, which was in flames. This was already towards the dusk. In his words, we would be safe, however I did not trust those words very much, and as I said, he told me that we did well to have surrendered the weapons, because otherwise we would fared the same as the village of Kovacevac. I did not comment on this. I just went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness BB, let me ask you a couple of questions of clarification. You mentioned a man by the name of Mario. Mario coming with two other men. Was Mario an HVO soldier, and how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform with insignia on the -- the HVO insignia on the left hand, and he had an automatic rifle, several rockets and he had one combat set, combat kit. They were shooting at villages of Merdani and Putis. I was alone in the house. My mother was at Jelinak in the village with her mother. My brother and sister. In fact, the youngest brother too had left the Jelinak village. They went to Nemila, which is beyond Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me ask you, Witness BB, you said you left the village of Jelinak. You were stopped by Stipo Andrijasevic or some soldiers at a location called Meraja. How many soldiers were at that location, Meraja and how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 30 soldiers there. I do not recall the exact number, but around that number. I noticed that three soldiers had, "HV", insignia whereas those who were from the Busovaca municipality had the HVO insignia so that meant to me that this was the Croatian army, but there was also some -- there were also some troops from Herzegovina there. And later I heard that indeed, a number of these soldiers took part. I also heard -- there were some murders in the area of Kula. I heard during the truce, that a brother of my professor, Ismet Medjuseljac, was killed and also some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to April 15th 1993. Could you please tell the judges about the circumstances of your arrest, and the arrest of other Muslims from the village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th April the shooting started around 6.30-7.00 pm. At that time I was in the village of Loncari. When I heard the shooting I started to go home, and before that I saw on television that a certain name called Totic had disappeared. I personally did not know him, and I am not sure whether this was true or not. So, I came home. I only managed to have some coffee and somebody was already knocking at the door. My sister came out, came back in tears, said, "some soldiers are looking for you". I came out. I could not recognise them because they had masks like stockings over their heads. Some had knit caps with just holes cut out for breathing and around them for eyes. I only recognised Pero. I cannot recall his name exactly. And somebody called Predo. He was a member of the MUP in Busovaca, and Pero was a neighbour in the village of Jelinak. Predo addressed me. He said something to the effect that we needed to go to Busovaca to have a conversation with Ivica Andrijasevic, son of Stipo, because Ivica was some kind of commander. We went with him. My brother was captured too. So we came down to the road below our house, then they started, they went to other houses so that they could get more men who were at their homes, but however, most of them were not around any more. Some of them had hidden, some of them had left. They got Nesib Osmancevic, Adil, and Kadir, who is a disabled person. He walked under his own power. He told me that there were other local villagers hidden in the basement of his house, so he immediately walked out and they aborted looking any further. They put us in a vehicle, and took us to the barracks of the -- or the former barracks at Kaonik. There they immediately searched us. They lined us up against a wall facing the wall, and we had to put our arms up and with our fingers spread out against a wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness BB, before we go into the events that took place at Kaonik, we only have a couple of minutes left and let me ask you a couple of questions of clarification on what you have just testified about. The men who arrested you at your home, arrested you and your brother and the others, were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you identified a number of people who were arrested, you named them. Were the people who were arrested all Muslim males?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the areas where you saw the HVO soldiers arresting these Muslims, was it on the road between Jelinak and the main road, the houses along that road between the main road and Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many HVO soldiers came to your house to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, 6 o'clock, I have concluded at this point my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, congratulations, Mr. Harmon, because you timed that well, and you are absolutely concise. I do not often congratulate you so I had better do it now. It is the purpose of your butting in, indeed, you have made it clear and tomorrow, this is for the interpreters, we shall start at 9.15 only. Thank you very much. The hearing is closed. (6.00 pm)
